analysis.one_liner: Provides public funding for House election campaigns, with $100 individual contribution limits.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or vote: it was referred to the House Administration Committee in June 2005 and died there when the 109th Congress ended, with zero cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have created a voluntary public financing system for House elections. Candidates who qualified — by collecting signatures from 3% of district voters or by belonging to a party that won over 25% of the last vote — would receive public funds of up to $750,000 (indexed to inflation), and in exchange could accept only small contributions of $100 or less from individuals, with 80% required to come from in-state donors [S2][S3]. The bill also added new disclosure rules for big spenders outside the campaigns and tightened rules on money funneled through intermediaries such as lobbyists [S2][S3]. It never moved beyond its referral to committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Candidates without access to large donors, and voters who want elections decided by residents rather than by big contributions. A qualifying candidate could run a fully funded campaign on public money and small donations instead of relying on wealthy donors and special interests, and the bill's debate requirement would have put candidates on television regardless of fundraising ability [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Qualifying House candidates receive public funds sized to the cost of about 2.5 hours of local television ad time, up to a $750,000 inflation-indexed maximum, so a candidate can reach voters without large donors [S3].

In exchange, candidates may accept only individual contributions of $100 or less per election cycle, with at least 80% from within the state, sharply reducing the influence of large donors and out-of-district money [S3].

The bill requires qualifying candidates to take part in at least two televised debates and forces broadcast stations to carry publicly funded advertising up to 40% of their airtime, with license renewal conditioned on compliance [S3].

New disclosure rules require any person spending over $2,000 on federal election activity to report it within 48 hours, and contributions routed through lobbyists and other intermediaries must be attributed to the true source [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers fund the program, and candidates who participate give up large contributions; large donors, lobbyists, and broadcast stations lose the ability to shape House elections through money and discretion over political advertising.

drawbacks.text: The program is taxpayer-funded, so public money is spent on political campaign advertising, which many taxpayers oppose [S2][S3].

The 3% signature threshold is a high hurdle in a large district, and requiring stations to devote up to 40% of airtime to political ads could impose real costs on broadcasters, whose licenses the bill holds hostage to compliance [S3].
The bill was voluntary, so candidates could still opt out and fund campaigns through large contributions, limiting how much it would actually reduce money in politics [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits — publicly funded campaigns, strict contribution limits, and faster disclosure of outside spending — come at a modest public cost and would apply only to candidates who choose to participate, so incumbents relying on large donations could simply stay outside the system. The design also raises practical questions about the signature threshold and the broadcaster mandate, but its core mechanism is a straightforward attempt to shift House elections from large donors to public funds and small donations.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced on June 7, 2005 and referred to the House Committee on House Administration, which never took it up, so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Robert Andrews (D-NJ) introduced the Public Campaign Financing Act of 2005 on June 7, 2005 [S1].
It was referred the same day to the House Committee on House Administration, and that was the bill's only action [S5].
No other member cosponsored the bill [S4].
The 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007, and the bill was never reported out of committee, given a hearing, or brought to a vote [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Incumbent House members and the large donors and special interests that fund them are better off, because the existing campaign financing system — large individual contributions, intermediary money, and undisclosed outside spending — continued unchanged. Broadcast stations likewise kept discretion over political advertising without the bill's airtime and license conditions.

for.name: Rep. Robert E. Andrews
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on June 7, 2005 and was its only sponsor, with no cosponsors joining [S1][S4].

against.name: House Committee on House Administration
against.role: Committee of referral for campaign finance legislation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on June 7, 2005 and took no further action on it — no markup, no hearing, no report — for the rest of the Congress [S5].

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Democratic sponsor and zero cosponsors from either party, so it never advanced far enough for any vote that would show how parties lined up [S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill would have forced stations to accept publicly funded political ad orders up to 40% of their airtime and conditioned license renewal on compliance, with random audits of ad rates [S3]. Their interest in keeping ad inventory and rate discretion ran against the bill's goal of guaranteeing candidates airtime.

The bill rewrites conduit rules so contributions arranged through lobbyists, foreign agents, and other intermediaries are attributed to the true source and reported [S3]. This reduces the value of bundling and conduit fundraising.

industries.industry: Large individual donors and wealthy campaign funders
industries.note: Participating candidates could accept at most $100 per individual per cycle, and 80% of contributions had to come from in-state donors, eliminating the leverage of large and out-of-district money [S3].
Any person spending more than $2,000 on federal election activity would have had to file a disclosure statement within 48 hours identifying whether it supported or opposed candidates [S3].
